title: AMD to Invest Tens of Billions in Global Supply Chain for AI Demand

tickers.name: SK hynix Inc. American Depositary Shares
Meta Platforms, Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
The chipmaker is scaling its manufacturing partnerships to address a persistent shortage of artificial intelligence processors. CEO Lisa Su announced AMD will invest 'tens of billions' of dollars throughout its global supply chain to satisfy compute demand that continues to exceed current capacity. The company is coordinating with production partners, including TSMC, Foxconn, Samsung, and SK Hynix, to substantially increase its chip supply by 2027 while addressing ongoing industry constraints in memory.

Shares of AMD rose about 2.7% as Citi raised its price target for the stock to $800 from $575, citing growth in CPU demand tied to Meta's Muse AI agent. The agent has passed 5 million downloads and runs on AMD silicon, which Morgan Stanley predicts could represent 20% of the company's chip sales in 2026. Citi estimates the market for 'always-on' agents may expand from $29B in 2025 to $300B by 2030.

selectedTweets.text:
$AMD CEO Lisa Su says demand is still running above supply and expects strong demand for compute to continue for the next several years, with AMD planning to “substantially increase” supply in 2027.

Su said AMD has already increased supply this year but “could definitely use more,” thanked TSMC for bringing additional capacity online, and noted that memory remains broadly supply constrained.

AMD is working with memory suppliers and customers to make sure capacity comes online together, while keeping its current business model unchanged.

Su also called Taiwan “very critical” to AMD and said the company plans to increase its investment there, while continuing to look at new packaging technologies.

Source: Reuters

selectedTweets.text:
AMD says demand is already higher than supply and this chart shows why 2027 could be even bigger.

Lisa Su says AMD will substantially increase chip supply next year as AI demand continues to exceed available capacity and AMD has already expanded supply throughout 2026, but management says it could still sell more chips if additional capacity were available. This chart shows how this could affect AMD’s server CPU business because it projects annual shipments increasing from fewer than 5 million units in 2023 to roughly 23 million by 2030, representing a compound annual growth rate of around 25%.

AMD could also benefit from higher prices. The chart projects server CPU average selling prices rising at approximately 9% annually and approaching $2,500 by 2030 as customers adopt larger, more powerful processors.
If unit shipments grow by 25% annually while average prices grow by 9%, AMD’s server CPU revenue could theoretically compound by roughly 36% annually.  AI servers do not run on GPUs alone, CPUs prepare data, coordinate accelerators, manage networking and storage, and handle the general purpose workloads surrounding AI models. As inference expands into more applications, data centers will need more CPUs alongside their GPUs. AMD could therefore benefit from several growth engines at once: more AI accelerators, rising EPYC server shipments, market share gains and higher average CPU prices.

The problem is no longer finding customers but rather securing enough advanced wafers, packaging capacity and memory to build complete systems. That is why Su traveled to Taiwan to meet key manufacturing partners and ensure CPU and GPU production can ramp together. AMD still has substantial room to grow across both CPUs and GPUs. Nvidia dominates AI accelerators but AMD does not need to overtake Nvidia for its business to expand dramatically. It only needs to capture part of a rapidly growing market while continuing to take share in server CPUs. Bullish on AMD.
